rationale: I'm replacing the 5 coarse relative bands with the full log-relative spectrum in 1 Hz bins (1–45 Hz) for each channel. Abnormal clinical EEG shows up as specific spectral shifts, such as focal or diffuse slowing, a slower alpha peak, and changes in beta and spindle bands, and fixed band edges blur these. The model is still L2 logistic regression, but C is now chosen by grouped inner CV on the training fold, since there are now about 836 features instead of 95.

The current features are all relative spectra, so they throw away overall amplitude. Many clinical abnormalities are partly amplitude findings: high-voltage diffuse or focal slowing, focal attenuation or suppression, and excess fast activity from medication. I'm adding the log absolute 1–45 Hz power of each channel (19 values per condition) next to the log-relative spectrum. Welch's median averaging makes that power estimate robust to the brief high-amplitude artifacts common in routine clinical recordings.

The current features describe each channel's spectrum separately, so they cannot see spatial structure: focal slowing confined to a few neighbouring channels, asymmetries between hemispheres, or loss of normal inter-channel coupling. This change adds the Log-Euclidean tangent-space vectors of band-limited spatial covariance matrices (delta, theta, alpha, beta). Each matrix is a log-domain mean of 2-s epoch covariances, which damps artifacts. Each epoch covariance is trace-normalized, so the features don't depend on amplitude scale, and shrunk to cope with the rank-deficient average reference. I have not run this version yet, so I have no score for it.

Clinical EEG abnormalities are often intermittent: bursts of focal or generalized slowing, epileptiform transients, and periods of attenuation. Averaging the spectrum and covariances over the whole recording blurs these out. This change adds per-channel time-variability features: over 2-s epochs, the std and 90th-percentile-minus-median of log relative band power (delta through gamma), plus the spread of log total power across epochs. Because these work on log ratios and log power spread, they don't depend on amplitude scale.

I'm making the score an equal-weight rank average of the current tuned L2 logistic regression and a regularized LightGBM trained on the same features. Clinical abnormality is often a nonlinear or conjunctive pattern, for example a slow alpha peak only when total power is high, or focal delta in one region only. A linear model can't express that, while a tree ensemble can, and its errors partly differ from the LR's, so averaging the two should raise AUROC. LightGBM uses fixed, conservative settings that I set by hand and did not tune against the dev score.

I'm adding per-channel waveform-shape statistics computed over 2-s epochs of the 1–45 Hz signal: kurtosis (median and 90th percentile across epochs), skewness of the signal and of its derivative, and Hjorth mobility and complexity. Spikes, sharp waves and other epileptiform or asymmetric morphology are phase-dependent features that the current features can't see, because spectra and covariances only capture second-order statistics. All of the new statistics are unaffected by amplitude scale. I haven't run this version, so I have no score for it.

Focal abnormalities (lateralized slowing, focal attenuation, unilateral excess beta) are among the most common reasons a clinical EEG is called abnormal, and they can appear on either hemisphere. A linear model on per-channel features can only learn signed left-minus-right contrasts, so slowing on the left and on the right cancel out. I'm adding sign-free asymmetry features: for 8 homologous electrode pairs, the |left − right| difference of log absolute and log relative band power in 5 bands (robust median Welch), plus the maximum over pairs per band. The features are ratio-based, so they don't depend on amplitude scale.

I'm adding weighted phase-lag index (wPLI) connectivity for the delta, theta, alpha and beta bands, taken from 2-s epoch cross-spectra and stored as the upper triangle of the channel-pair matrix. The current covariance features only capture zero-lag (in-phase) coupling, which is dominated by volume conduction and the shared average reference. wPLI keeps only lagged, non-zero-phase coupling, which should pick up the disrupted or abnormally increased long-range synchronization of encephalopathy and focal lesions, information the existing features don't have. It is unaffected by amplitude scale and by any reference that is added identically to all channels, which matters for the external datasets.

This adds a complexity/entropy feature family the model doesn't have yet. For each channel, on 4-s epochs of the 1–45 Hz signal, I compute multiscale ordinal-pattern (permutation) entropy at order 4 with delays of 10, 20 and 40 ms, plus the Higuchi fractal dimension, using both the median and the 10th percentile across epochs. Encephalopathy, diffuse or focal slowing and rhythmic or epileptiform activity all make the signal more regular in ways that are nonlinear and depend on phase. These features don't depend on amplitude scale or on a shared reference offset, and they are cheap to compute. This version has not been run, so it has no score yet.

I'm adding explicit spectral parameterization, a lightweight FOOOF-style decomposition. Two clinical criteria for an abnormal background are a posterior dominant rhythm slowed below about 8 Hz and a steeper (more "slow") 1/f background. The current features only approximate these, through fixed 1-Hz relative bins and linear weights. For each channel I fit a robust aperiodic line in log–log space over 2–40 Hz (median Welch, 4-s windows, 0.25-Hz resolution), giving the exponent and offset. Above that line I take the peak frequency, peak height and the periodic power in each band, plus the median peak frequency over posterior channels and over all channels. The exponent, peak frequency and periodic power above the line don't depend on amplitude scale.

I'm adding a third ensemble member: an RBF-kernel SVM trained on standardized features, clipped to ±5 SD to limit outliers from artifacts. Its C is chosen by grouped inner CV on the training fold, and the final score is the equal-weight rank average of LR, LightGBM and SVM. Abnormality patterns in this feature space are partly nonlinear but smooth, for example several mild deviations combining across spectral, covariance and waveform features. A kernel machine models that differently from both the linear model and the axis-aligned trees, so its errors should be partly independent and the average should be more accurate. This version has not been run, so there is no score for it yet.

The per-channel log-relative 1-Hz spectrum, the largest feature block, currently comes from mean-averaged Welch. In routine clinical recordings, eye blinks and eye movements inflate frontal delta, and muscle bursts inflate temporal beta and gamma, which hides the background rhythm the abnormal/normal call depends on. I'm switching that spectrum to median-averaged Welch, the same artifact-robust estimator the absolute-power and asymmetry features already use. Intermittent abnormal events are still captured by the epoch-variability features. This version has not been run, so it has no dev score yet.

The spatial covariance features gave by far the biggest gain so far (+0.039), but they use only four broad bands and leave out 30–45 Hz. I'm switching them to nine finer bands: 1–2, 2–4, 4–6, 6–8, 8–10, 10–13, 13–20, 20–30 and 30–45 Hz. The finer bands keep apart spatial patterns that clinically mean different things and currently get averaged together: polymorphic slow delta vs. faster rhythmic delta, posterior alpha slowed into 6–8 Hz vs. a normal alpha topography, low vs. high (drug-related) beta, and the scalp distribution of temporal/frontal muscle activity at 30–45 Hz.
I'm adding about 29 location-invariant "worst-channel" summaries derived from the per-channel features we already compute. They are:

Clinical abnormalities such as intermittent focal or rhythmic slowing change the spatial pattern of the EEG only some of the time, and the Log-Euclidean mean covariance averages that variation away. I'm adding, for each band, how far each 2-s epoch's log-covariance sits from the recording's mean: the log of the median and of the 90th-percentile Frobenius distance. I'm also adding, per channel, the standard deviation across epochs of that channel's log share of band power. These are cheap to compute because the per-epoch matrices already exist, and they don't depend on amplitude scale because each covariance is trace-normalized. This version hasn't been run, so it has no dev score yet.

I'm changing where the covariance features are projected. Right now each recording's band covariance is projected at the identity matrix. Instead, I'll take the Riemannian (affine-invariant) mean of all recordings' band covariances as the reference point, whiten each recording by it, and take the log (Riemannian re-centering). This should separate deviations in spatial structure better than the identity reference, since the covariance block gave the biggest gain so far (+0.039). The reference uses no labels, and it re-centers each dataset that is featurized, which should help on external amplifiers and references.

The tree slot of the ensemble becomes the rank-average of the existing LightGBM and a CatBoost model. CatBoost's ordered boosting and symmetric (oblivious) trees are more strongly regularized and less prone to overfitting with ~2.7k recordings and ~2.1k correlated features. Its errors should be only partly correlated with LightGBM's leaf-wise trees, so the tree-based view of conjunctive abnormality patterns should be more accurate and stable. The overall LR / trees / SVM weighting stays at one-third each. CatBoost uses fixed settings I chose by hand, not tuned on the dev score.

The last attempt (CatBoost) timed out, so this change adds little compute. It adds a 5th band, 30–45 Hz, to the Log-Euclidean covariance block, which has given the largest gain so far. The hypothesis is that the scalp layout of high-frequency activity carries signal for abnormality, and none of the current covariance bands cover it: diffuse drug-related fast activity, focal fast activity over skull defects, and the temporal/frontal muscle activity seen in less cooperative abnormal patients. To stay well inside the time limit, I also compute the median Welch spectrum and the 1–45 Hz band-passed signal once per recording and reuse them, instead of recomputing each 2–3 times. This refactor leaves every existing feature unchanged.

Add features from a bipolar "double-banana" montage, which is the 18-derivation montage TUH neurologists read when labelling these recordings. For each derivation I compute the log relative power in 9 fine bands, the log total power (median Welch), and the existing scale-free waveform statistics (kurtosis, skew of the signal and its derivative, Hjorth). The average reference spreads focal slowing and sharp transients across all channels, while bipolar derivations pick up local potential gradients, where focal abnormalities and phase-reversing spikes show up most clearly. The log-mapped, trace-normalized covariances keep spatial structure but do not give these local band powers or local waveform shapes directly.

I'm adding Log-Euclidean tangent-space covariance features for the bipolar double-banana montage in the delta, theta, alpha and beta bands. They reuse the band-filtered signals that are already computed, so the extra cost is small. Neurologists find focal abnormalities through phase reversals, which appear as anti-correlation between neighbouring derivations in a chain that share an electrode. They also look for local slowing gradients. The covariance of the average-referenced channels holds this information only indirectly, and so do the per-derivation bipolar band powers, which carry no cross-derivation structure. Bipolar covariance feeds this local-gradient coupling directly to all three models. It is also reference-free and trace-normalized, so it should hold up on external datasets with different amplitude scales and references. This version has not been run, so I have no dev score for it yet.
